newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-RBA cut official interest rates.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-RBA cut official interest rates.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia made a surprise 50 basis points cut in official interest rates to 6.0 percent on Wednesday.
The market had expected the central bank to keep policy on hold until early next year after it left rates on hold after last week's monthly board meeting.
The following is a selection of economists' immediate reactions to the announcement.
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"A little surprised as to the timing. We had thought that if there were to be another rate cut it would have been in February rather than in December. The bank may have been concerned to avoid tying the timing of decisions to the day after meetings, but it's more likely been driven by a change to the bank's outlook for inflation following the release of the national accounts earlier this month."
CHRIS CATON, ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"We were expecting this in early February after the next round of inflation data. The growth outlook for the economy is quite weak and inflation news is good so this is the right decision, it's just a little earlier then we thought it was going to be. This is possibily the last cut, we will get some pickup in growth over the course next year. Monetary policy history is littered with examples of one too many moves. This wasn't the one too many move, but the next one might be."
PETER HORN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, SBC WARURG:

"Surprised that they didn't wait until the February board meeting. I thought they might have wanted to get a little more confirmation on the economy. I am not surprised with their view on inflation. We know the inflation outlook is extremely good and that inflation expectations have been falling. I'm surprised they didn't wait a little longer to see the impact of the previous rate cuts. In all probability (the last rate cut), unless the economy deteriorates from here."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"There may be an element of panic in this cut. It may have been more sensible to wait for the December quarter CPI data to confirm the low inflation outlook. They must be more concerned about the economy than we thought, and particularly employment. The exchange rate has been a factor by pressuring inflation but I don't think they've allowed enough time to see the impact of the last two rate cuts. But now that they're expecting inflation to stay low and, as long as the exchnage rate remains relatively firm, you can't even rule out further cuts down the road."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"We've been calling for it, so we're glad that it's come. It will hopefully provide a stimulus and help ensure the government's economic forecasts are obtained. We didn't think they could act that quickly. We believe that this may well be the end of the cycle."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH:

"It's a bit of surprise -- no surprise about interest rates being cut again, the surprise is the timing of it. I suppose at the end of the day the bank thought if they were going to cut again why wait until the end of February. Six percent is probably a reasonably comfortable level for the bank, but my suspicion is their aiming to get it down to 5.5 percent."
TIM PFITZNER, ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"The timing is certainly a surprise, the direction and magnitude are not. We'd expected that maybe they'd wait for next year. But the things they've highlighted, low inflationary expectations, price deflators in national accounts ... pointed to a cut in official rates. And the one thing they've highlighted here is the strength of the Aussie dollar."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER INTERNATIONAL:

"We thought there was a 50/50 chance of another cut, but certainly the timing has come a lot earlier than we thought. The inflation outlook has improved over the last few months and certainly the economy is weak so in a sense this rate cut does not cause any danger down the track for inflation. I think it's too early to tell (if it will be the last cut). Obviously there will be another assessment when the board meets in February. It depends what the signs are in terms of the impact of the rate cuts already, whether or not they will move again. I still think it as a 50/50 chance of another cut. It depends what happens in between times."
